title: code-review-pr-scratchpad-tae-lee
content:
PR: refactor kv-cache eviction + async batching (https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/482)
Author: @marcos-santos
Goal: clean up eviction logic, add batched eviction API, and make eviction asynchronous to avoid blocking token generation loop.
Context: this is a follow-up to the kv-cache perf work (ENG-1230). The previous approach had synchronous eviction under memory pressure which caused occasional latency spikes. PR tries to decouple eviction by pushing to an async worker and expose a BatchEvict API to reduce lock contention.

Quick summary of changes:
- Extracted eviction logic into kv/evict_manager.go (EvictManager + worker pool)
- Added BatchEvict(ctx, keys[]) on KVCache interface
- Switched callers in runtime/token_streamer.go to enqueue keys instead of immediate evict
- Added metrics: kv_evict_queue_len, kv_evict_worker_errors_total
- Tests: unit tests for EvictManager; integration test that simulates memory pressure (flaky locally)

My quick read (first pass):
- overall approach makes sense (decouple blocking work)
- signs of shrink-wrapped complexity: worker pool + backpressure + batching + retry heuristics all in one file -> hard to reason about

Checklist (high level) - to tick off during review:
- [ ] Behavior preserves correctness (no stale keys)
- [ ] No regression in hot-path latency under normal load
- [ ] Memory pressure path actually reduces blocking (bench/sim)
- [ ] Metrics are meaningful and have good cardinality
- [ ] Tests stable and deterministic (flaky tests = blocker)
- [ ] Documentation / comments for new public API (BatchEvict)
- [ ] CI passes, static analysis ok (go vet/golint)

Potential correctness concerns / questions to ask author:
1) Evict timing guarantees: does BatchEvict guarantee eventual eviction? Is there a retry/backoff strategy? What if worker pool is saturated and queue keeps growing -- will we apply backpressure upstream or drop keys?
2) Stale reads: If a token generation request expects a recent eviction to have happened (rare), could async eviction create a window where KVCache returns evicted-but-not-yet-removed items? Need to confirm consistency model.
3) Locking: original implementation used cache-level lock for eviction; new code uses per-shard locks plus queue. Verify there are no subtle races (look for double-checked deletes or missing barrier).
4) Error handling: worker errors are incremented in metric, but are they surfaced to caller? Should we have a hard-fail mode for critical customers (config flag?)

Refactor / improvement ideas (notes-to-self and possible recommendations):
- Separate responsibilities: EvictManager should be a thin orchestrator that delegates batching strategy + worker pool configuration to collaborators. Right now it does both scheduling and the batch aggregation logic. Consider extracting BatchAggregator interface (strategy pattern) -> easier to test.
- Backpressure semantics: instead of unbounded queue, add a bounded channel + offer/drop policy with metrics. If queue full, record dropped_eviction_keys_total and maybe fallback to immediate eviction for high-priority callers.
- Make batching pluggable: different workloads might prefer small immediate batches vs larger delayed batches. Expose config via runtime config (json) or flags on Dedicated.
- Add a synchronous fallback API (EvictSync) used by low-QPS/high-consistency routes (example: model fine-tune eviction hooks)
- Centralize retries: current code retries n times per batch; move to a retrier util with jittered backoff and circuit-breaker to avoid hot-looping on persistent errors.

Testing / bench ideas:
- Microbench: synthetic workload with N keys evicted per second and M concurrent generators; measure p50/p95 latency change with old vs new approach.
- Load test: run in QA with real LLM request mix (~30s sequences) and simulate memory pressure to validate no spike.
- Deterministic test for async worker: use a fake clock + deterministic channel scheduling to assert eventual eviction and error paths. Current integration test flaky locally -> convert to table-driven unit tests with injected backpressure.

Specific code comments to leave inline (locations approximate):
- kv/evict_manager.go: EvictManager.run() line ~120: losing context cancellation when using time.After -> switch to time.Ticker with select on ctx.Done to avoid goroutine leak.
- kv/evict_manager.go: batching logic: hard-coded batch size 512 -> prefer constant + comment why 512 chosen; make configurable.
- runtime/token_streamer.go: callers enqueue keys with nil checks missing (possible nil slice enqueue). Add defensive check and metric for invalid enqueues.
- tests/kv_evict_test.go: use t.Parallel() where safe. Remove sleep(500ms) in favor of channel sync signals to reduce flakiness.

Follow-ups (post-merge / optional):
- Add e2e benchmark job in infra/perf that runs nightly comparing old vs new eviction (ENG-1372 follow-up).
- Add a small dashboard tile in Console for kv_evict_queue_len and worker errors with alert if queue_len > threshold for 5m.
- Discuss tuning defaults for Dedicated customers in config doc.

Draft PR comment blocks (short):
- "Nice separation of concerns — decoupling eviction from hot-path is the right move. A few correctness questions below about eventual eviction guarantees and backpressure semantics. Also, tests are flaky locally; let's make them deterministic before merging."
- "Consider extracting batching strategy into a separate component to simplify EvictManager and make unit testing easier."

Notes to self for next pass (personal TODOs):
- Run local microbench comparing old vs new on my dev GPU (vector of 1000 concurrent requests) -> record p95 difference.
- Reproduce flaky integration test: run 10x CI locally to capture failure trace, then convert to deterministic unit test.
- Draft a proposed interface change for BatchEvict to support priorities (high/low) and synchronous fallback.
- Pair with @marcos-santos to walk through the run loop and error paths; schedule 30m sync.

Quick links for reviewer context:
- Original design notes (confluence): https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/ENG/KV+Cache+Eviction+Design
- Related PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/411 (kv cache v1)
- Github PR under review: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/482

Random scratch thoughts (unpolished):
- Is there any value in hooking eviction decisions to model memory map (size-per-token) rather than number-of-keys? Could prioritize eviction by estimated memory delta. Might be heavy.
- If eviction backlog becomes common, maybe autoscale a dedicated eviction pool on Dedicated customers (configurable) - treat it like background maintenance work.
- Make metrics taggable by tenant so we can see per-customer eviction pressure (but careful with high cardinality)

END
